name: Fred Rogers
tagline: A shy, bullied boy who made plain, daily kindness his life's craft on television.
startedFrom: He was born in 1928 in Latrobe, Pennsylvania, into a very wealthy family: his father ran manufacturing firms in the town, and a chauffeur picked him up from school. As a boy he was overweight, shy and sickly, sometimes kept at home by illness, and other children chased him and called him 'fat Freddy'. Adults told him to pretend he did not care, so nobody would bother him.

evidence.claim: Before the US Senate he described his work as giving 'an expression of care every day to each child, to help him realize that he is unique'.
evidence.locator: Testimony, Senate Subcommittee on Communications, 1 May 1969

evidence.claim: David Newell, who played Mr. McFeely on the show, said on the day Rogers died: 'He was so genuinely, genuinely kind, a wonderful person.'
evidence.locator: paragraph quoting family spokesman David Newell

evidence.claim: The Fred Rogers Institute at Saint Vincent College, which holds his archive of over 20,000 items, says he was known for his creativity, kindness, spirituality and commitment to children.

At seventy he still swam nearly every morning, rose at 5:30 to read, study, write and pray, went to bed at 9:30, and did not drink, smoke or eat meat; he had kept his weight at 143 pounds for about thirty-one years.
evidence.locator: passages on his morning swim, his weight of 143 pounds and his daily schedule

evidence.claim: Guitarist Joe Negri, who worked on the show, called him 'certainly a perfectionist' who refused to accept shoddy ad-libbing from guests.
The AP obituary reports that off the set he swam daily and read voraciously.
Former Post-Gazette reporter Tim Reeves wrote that Rogers invited him to swim early morning laps with him at the Pittsburgh Athletic Association, 'a discipline he treasured'.
evidence.locator: passage quoting Tim Reeves on swimming laps at the Pittsburgh Athletic Association

evidence.claim: He earned a divinity degree at Pittsburgh Theological Seminary while working in television, and was ordained by the United Presbyterian Church with the charge to work with children and their families through the mass media.
He once volunteered at a state prison in Pittsburgh and helped set up a playroom there for children visiting their parents.

In his 1999 Television Academy interview he said he would like to be remembered as a compassionate human being who was lucky to be born when television could let him use all the talents he had been given.
evidence.locator: interview page, 'About' quotation; chapter 10, 'On how he'd like to be remembered'

evidence.claim: Accepting his Lifetime Achievement Emmy in 1997, he used his speech to ask the audience for ten seconds of silence to think of the people who had helped them become who they are, and timed it himself.
evidence.locator: Lifetime Achievement acceptance, 24th Daytime Emmy Awards, Radio City Music Hall, 21 May 1997

evidence.claim: At Dartmouth in 2002 he said that 'we just don't get to be competent human beings without a lot of different investments from others', and asked the graduates for a silent minute to think of those people.
evidence.locator: Commencement address, Dartmouth College, June 2002, paragraphs after the Little Prince passage

evidence.claim: He completed a bachelor of divinity at Pittsburgh Theological Seminary in 1962 and was ordained a Presbyterian minister.
evidence.locator: biographical summary and Bio, fourth paragraph

evidence.claim: Each morning he rose early to pray for the many people who had asked for his prayers.
evidence.locator: passage beginning 'The first time I called Mister Rogers on the telephone'

evidence.claim: The Fred Rogers Institute's archivist says the archive shows that Mister Rogers was not a character separate from Fred but 'Fred's way of ministering to children and families'.

principles.text: Thank the people who helped make you, and give others a moment to remember theirs.
Feelings, anger included, can be named and handled; you can stop yourself and do something else instead.
principles.locator: Testimony, 1 May 1969, on 'mentionable and manageable' feelings and the song 'What do you do with the mad that you feel?'

principles.text: Do not pretend you do not care, even when people tell you it would be safer.
principles.locator: section 'On Rogers being bullied as a child'

principles.text: Keep the same plain daily habits, year after year: rise early, swim, sleep on time.
principles.locator: passages on his morning swim and daily schedule

principles.text: Nobody has to do anything sensational to be loved; treat people that way.
principles.locator: Commencement address, June 2002, passage after the song 'It's You I Like'

quotes.text: I give an expression of care every day to each child, to help him realize that he is unique.
quotes.locator: Testimony, Senate Subcommittee on Communications, Washington, 1 May 1969

quotes.text: …if we in public television can only make it clear that feelings are mentionable and manageable, we will have done a great service for mental health.
quotes.locator: Testimony, Senate Subcommittee on Communications, Washington, 1 May 1969

quotes.text: All of us have special ones who have loved us into being.
quotes.locator: Lifetime Achievement acceptance, 24th Daytime Emmy Awards, New York, 21 May 1997

quotes.text: You don't ever have to do anything sensational for people to love you.

definingMoment.text: On 1 May 1969 he testified to a US Senate subcommittee as a proposal stood to cut federal funding for public broadcasting from $20 million to $10 million. Its chairman, Senator John Pastore, seemed gruff and impatient when he gave him the floor. Rogers declined to read his written statement, spoke for about six minutes about children's feelings, and recited the words of his song 'What do you do with the mad that you feel?'. Pastore said it was the first time he had had goose bumps in two days, and that Rogers had just earned the $20 million.

shadow.text: François Clemmons, who played Officer Clemmons on the show from 1968, writes in his 2020 memoir that Rogers called him into his office after being told Clemmons had been seen at a gay bar. By Clemmons's account, Rogers said it did not matter to him personally if Clemmons was gay, but that he could not be out as gay and stay an important member of the show. Clemmons writes that Rogers then asked whether he had thought of getting married, and that by the time he left the office he had decided to marry a woman; they divorced in 1974.

councilQuestion.text: When you felt angry this week, did you name it and choose what to do with it, or did it choose for you?

screen.notes: A real American television host and Presbyterian minister (1928-2003), never a politician or candidate, founded no religion; searches by name found no credible account (no court record, suit or named accuser) of sexual contact with anyone under 16 or of sexual violence; his documented dark side is that, by his cast member François Clemmons's account, he told Clemmons he could not be out as gay and stay on the show.

review.devilsAdvocate: I attacked each value against the Senate testimony, the Emmy and Dartmouth speeches, Esquire 1998, the AP obituary and the Fred Rogers Institute, and searched for a darker side beyond Clemmons's account; none with a reputable source turned up. Faith, Service and Gratitude are shared with the blind pick; Kindness held on three sources, and Discipline held once a third, the Post-Gazette's Tim Reeves account, was added. All four quotes match his own transcripts; the defining moment now rests on WETA instead of a Facebook-sourced magazine item, and three small facts were corrected.
